paragraphs.heading: Messages between cells
paragraphs.text: Cell signaling is the way a cell deals with its surroundings, with other cells and even with itself, and every form of life does it. A signal usually involves three parts: a first messenger called a ligand, a receptor, and the signal itself. Most signals are chemicals, molecules that can bind to and switch on a particular receptor. Ligands come in many kinds, from ions such as Na⁺, K⁺ and Ca²⁺ to lipids, peptides such as insulin, and carbohydrates. Some signals are physical instead, such as pressure, voltage, temperature or light.

paragraphs.heading: Getting through the membrane
paragraphs.text: Peptide and lipid ligands are especially important, since most hormones fall into those two groups. Peptides usually cannot slip freely through the lipid bilayer of the plasma membrane, because they are polar, hydrophilic molecules. Instead they act through receptors fixed in the membrane. Fat-soluble chemicals such as steroid hormones can drift straight through the membrane and meet receptors inside the cell.

paragraphs.heading: Near and far
paragraphs.text: Signals are sorted by where they act. In autocrine signaling a cell responds to a chemical it made itself, and in intracrine signaling that chemical acts on receptors in the cell's own cytoplasm or nucleus. Juxtacrine signaling passes between cells that sit right next to each other, and paracrine signaling between cells close by. Endocrine signaling links distant cells, usually through a hormone carried in the blood.

paragraphs.heading: Receptors
paragraphs.text: Receptors are complex proteins, found either in the plasma membrane or inside the cell. Each detects a signal by binding a specific chemical or by changing shape when a physical agent acts on it, and this precise match is what lets a ligand trigger one particular response. Membrane receptors come in three main types. Ion channel receptors work a gate that allows or blocks certain ions. G-protein coupled receptors grab a ligand with their outer part and set off a chain of chemical reactions with their inner part, and enzyme-linked receptors have an inner part that acts as an enzyme.

paragraphs.heading: Receptors inside the cell
paragraphs.text: Intracellular receptors work differently. They usually bind fat-soluble ligands, such as steroid hormones, that have passed through the membrane on their own. The hormone is then carried into the nucleus, where certain genes are switched on and the cell builds certain proteins.

paragraphs.heading: Passing the signal on
paragraphs.text: Once the signal meets its receptor, signal transduction begins: a series of molecular events inside the cell that leads to the final effect. Often that effect is opening an ion channel or starting a second messenger system, a cascade that spreads the signal through the cell. Second messengers can amplify a signal, since switching on a few receptors can activate many secondary messengers.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Each cell is set up to answer particular signals from outside, and this underlies development, tissue repair, immunity and homeostasis. When signaling goes wrong, it can cause diseases such as cancer, autoimmunity and diabetes. Bacteria signal too. Through quorum sensing, individuals start an activity only once their population is large enough; the marine bacterium Aliivibrio fischeri, where this was first seen, makes light only when its population is dense enough.
